analysis.one_liner: Lets consumer product safety regulators set safety standards for firearms and firearm components.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have ended firearms' exemption from consumer product safety regulation, died in committee with zero cosponsors and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Firearms are currently the only major consumer product excluded from the Consumer Product Safety Commission, the agency that sets safety standards and orders recalls for things like cribs, toys, and stoves. This bill would have struck that exclusion, letting the commission write safety standards for guns and gun components and act on defective models. It never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee with no cosponsors until the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Gun owners and their families, who would gain protection against defective firearms — guns that fire when dropped, misfire, or otherwise malfunction — through mandatory safety standards and recalls. The Consumer Product Safety Commission would gain authority over a product category it is currently barred from touching.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the exclusion that keeps pistols, revolvers, and other firearms outside the Consumer Product Safety Act's definition of a consumer product, so the safety commission could issue mandatory standards for them for the first time.

Grants the commission explicit rulemaking authority over firearms, which in practice means the power to require design fixes and order recalls of defective guns and components, the same way it handles other dangerous consumer products.

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers, importers, and dealers would bear the cost of testing, redesign, and recalls to meet any new safety standards. Some of those costs would likely be passed on to buyers as higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Safety standards address defects, not misuse: a gun that works exactly as designed would still pass, so the bill would do little about the majority of gun deaths and injuries, which come from intentional violence and accidents with functioning firearms rather than defective ones.

The grant of authority is broad — it covers firearms generally, not just clearly defective models — so manufacturers and their allies argued it could be used to impose design restrictions that raise costs and prices far beyond fixing genuine defects, an honest cost an supporter would have to weigh.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrower than the bill's framing suggests: it targets defective firearms, a genuine gap since guns are the only major consumer product the safety commission cannot touch, but it would not address most gun violence. The costs — testing, redesign, recalls, and modestly higher prices — are the same costs every other consumer product maker already absorbs under safety rules. On balance a modest, targeted improvement that was never seriously pursued: it drew zero cosponsors, including from gun-safety Democrats, and died without a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, sat there with no cosponsors, and the congressional term ended without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced the bill on June 21, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Two days later it was sent to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, where it stayed; no hearing, markup, or floor action followed for the rest of the 118th Congress.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors in either chamber, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers, who keep their exemption from consumer product safety regulation and face no mandatory standards or recalls for defective guns. No one else gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firearms manufacturers keeping their safety-rule exemption

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter in Congress; no member signed on as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, routed it to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, and never scheduled a hearing or markup for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Firearms industry groups (NRA, National Shooting Sports Foundation)
against.what_they_did: Long opposed giving the Consumer Product Safety Commission any jurisdiction over firearms, viewing safety standards as a route to design restrictions; their opposition shaped the lack of congressional appetite for the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; the bill's only support was a single House Democrat, with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: Guns are the only major consumer product exempt from Consumer Product Safety Commission standards and recalls; this bill would have ended that exemption, exposing manufacturers to mandatory safety standards and defect recalls for the first time. The industry's interest in avoiding oversight runs directly against buyers' interest in safer products.

Dealers could face recall obligations and inventory restrictions if the commission set standards or found models defective, and would bear minor compliance costs. The burden is smaller than manufacturers' but flows from the same lost exemption.
